notes.h: What incomplete dominance is (Higher Level only)
notes.b: With complete dominance, one allele (a version of a gene) hides the other in a heterozygote (an organism carrying two different alleles). With incomplete dominance, neither allele hides the other, and the results of crosses look different.
points: The heterozygote's phenotype (its observable feature) lies between those of the two homozygotes (organisms with two identical alleles), e.g. pink snapdragons from red × white.
There are three phenotypes rather than two, so each genotype (the pair of alleles an organism carries) can be recognised just by looking at the phenotype.
With complete dominance the heterozygote looks like the homozygous dominant (Tt is as tall as TT), so there are only two phenotypes and a tall plant could be TT or Tt.
The AB blood group is not an example of incomplete dominance: both the A and B antigens are fully made side by side, rather than giving an in-between result.
notes.tip: If asked to explain the term, say the heterozygote shows a phenotype between the two homozygous phenotypes because neither allele is fully dominant. Don't offer AB blood group as an example.

notes.h: Why the heterozygote is pink (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The pink colour has a simple molecular cause, which also shows that the alleles themselves are never altered.
points: In snapdragon flower colour, the red allele codes for a working enzyme that makes red pigment, and the white allele codes for no working pigment enzyme.
A plant with two red alleles has two working copies, so it makes enough pigment to be red.
A heterozygote has only one working copy, so it makes less pigment and is pink. A plant with two white alleles makes none and is white.
The alleles are not mixed or changed: red and white flowers reappear in the next generation, which shows the genes themselves do not blend.
notes.tip: Incomplete dominance is not blending inheritance. Say that the alleles stay separate and the parental phenotypes reappear in the offspring of two pink plants.

notes.h: Symbols for incompletely dominant alleles (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Genetics questions need a key for the allele letters. A capital and lower-case pair suggests one allele is dominant, so incomplete dominance needs a different choice.
points: Neither allele is dominant, so don't use a capital and a lower-case letter of the same kind as if one were dominant.
Use the letters the question gives.
If choosing, use two different capital letters, e.g. R = allele for red, W = allele for white (so RR red, RW pink, WW white), and state in the key that the alleles show incomplete dominance.
Questions sometimes use B and b with a statement that B is incompletely dominant; follow the question's key.
notes.tip: Pink is the heterozygote, so write it as RW. Don't write pink as RR or invent a separate allele 'P'.

notes.h: First cross: homozygous × homozygous (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Snapdragon flower colour. Crossing a true-breeding red plant with a true-breeding white plant is the simplest cross, and it shows where the pink phenotype comes from.
points: Key: R = red, W = white, incomplete dominance.
Parents' phenotypes: red × white.
Parents' genotypes: RR × WW.
Gametes (sex cells, each carrying one allele): R × W.
Offspring genotypes: all RW, because every offspring gets one R from one parent and one W from the other.
Offspring phenotypes: all (100%) pink.

notes.h: Second cross: heterozygote × heterozygote (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Crossing two pink plants brings the parental colours back, which is the classic test of incomplete dominance. Set it out in the standard layout, line by line.
points: Parents' phenotypes: pink × pink.
Parents' genotypes: RW × RW.
Gametes: R, W × R, W, because each parent can pass on either of its two alleles.
Punnett square (a grid showing every possible combination of gametes): RR, RW / RW, WW.
Offspring genotypes: 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW.
Offspring phenotypes: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (25% red, 50% pink, 25% white).
Diagram: draw the 2 × 2 Punnett square for RW × RW. Labels: gametes R and W on each side; boxes RR, RW, RW, WW; each box labelled red, pink, pink or white (or shaded red, pink, white).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to use a cross to give the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring of two heterozygotes, with the ratio. Show every line: key, parents, gametes, square, genotypes, phenotypes.

notes.h: Recognising incomplete dominance from the ratio (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The offspring ratio of a heterozygote × heterozygote cross tells you which kind of dominance a trait shows.
points: The phenotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) is the same as the genotype ratio, because each genotype has its own phenotype.
With complete dominance the same cross gives 3 : 1, because the heterozygote looks like the dominant homozygote and the two classes merge.
If a cross of two parents that look the same gives three phenotypes in a 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, the trait shows incomplete dominance.
notes.tip: Exams ask how the ratio would differ if one allele were completely dominant: 3 : 1 instead of 1 : 2 : 1. With incomplete dominance 1 : 2 : 1 is the phenotype ratio; with complete dominance it is only the genotype ratio.

notes.b: A pink plant can also be crossed with a red or a white one. Only two genotypes are possible in the offspring, so there are two phenotypes in a 1 : 1 ratio.
points: Parents' genotypes: RW × WW (pink × white).
Gametes: R, W × W, because the homozygous parent can only pass on W.
Offspring genotypes: 1 RW : 1 WW.
Offspring phenotypes: 1 pink : 1 white.
Pink × red: RW × RR gives 1 RR : 1 RW, so 1 red : 1 pink.

notes.h: Second example: Andalusian fowl (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Chickens give a second example of incomplete dominance, with a practical consequence for breeders.
points: In Andalusian chickens, feather colour shows incomplete dominance.
Homozygous black × homozygous white gives all offspring with grey-blue feathers, called 'blue'.
Blue × blue gives 1 black : 2 blue : 1 white.
If black were instead completely dominant to white, the same blue-type (heterozygous) cross would give 3 black : 1 white.
Blue Andalusians can never be true-breeding (always producing offspring like themselves), because every blue bird is heterozygous and its offspring include black and white.
Breeders get all-blue chicks by crossing black with white birds.
notes.tip: Exams use feather colour in Andalusian fowl as the trait for a cross of two heterozygotes. Give genotypes, phenotypes and the 1 : 2 : 1 ratio, and be ready to state the 3 : 1 ratio for complete dominance.

notes.h: Combining with a second gene (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Real organisms carry many genes at once, so a cross can follow an incompletely dominant gene together with a completely dominant one.
points: A cross can combine an incompletely dominant gene with a completely dominant one, e.g. snapdragon flower colour with plant height.
This is a two-gene cross. There is more on this in Dihybrid crosses, which has the worked example.
notes.tip: Exams can ask for a two-gene cross with one incompletely dominant gene and one dominant gene. Use the correct key for each gene.

keyTerms.definition: A pattern of inheritance in which the heterozygote's phenotype lies between those of the two homozygotes, so there are three phenotypes.
A plant (Antirrhinum majus) whose flower colour shows incomplete dominance: red × white gives all pink.
A chicken with grey-blue feathers, from a cross of black and white birds; it is heterozygous and does not breed true.

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by incomplete dominance, using a named example.
questions.model: Incomplete dominance is when the heterozygote's phenotype lies between those of the two homozygotes, so there are three phenotypes rather than two. In snapdragon flower colour, red (RR) and white (WW) plants give pink heterozygotes (RW), because the red allele codes for a working enzyme that makes red pigment, while the white allele codes for no working pigment enzyme. A heterozygote has only one working copy, so it makes less pigment and is pink. The alleles are not blended: red and white flowers reappear in the next generation.

questions.prompt: In snapdragons, red flower (R) and white flower (W) show incomplete dominance. Using a genetic cross, show the genotypes and phenotypes of the offspring of two pink-flowered plants and give the phenotype ratio.
questions.model: Key: R = red, W = white, incomplete dominance. Parents' phenotypes: pink × pink. Parents' genotypes: RW × RW. Gametes: R, W × R, W. Punnett square: RR, RW / RW, WW. Offspring genotypes: 1 RR : 2 RW : 1 WW. Offspring phenotypes: 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white (25% red, 50% pink, 25% white).

questions.prompt: Two blue Andalusian chickens are crossed. Give the expected phenotype ratio and explain how this ratio would differ if black feathers were completely dominant to white.
questions.model: Blue × blue gives 1 black : 2 blue : 1 white. The blue chickens are heterozygous, so each parent gives black and white alleles in equal numbers, and the three genotypes each have their own phenotype. If black were completely dominant to white, the heterozygous blue birds would look black, so the same cross would give 3 black : 1 white instead.
